Three years ago, I walked into my first Conference on Indonesia Foreign Policy (CIFP ) by FPCI  as a hotelier who wasn’t sure he belonged in the room. 

Last Saturday at the 10th edition of CIFP, I was back for my third time, and I realised how much that room has taught me.

Foreign policy is not my expertise. 

But year after year, FPCI has shown me that what is decided in diplomatic halls eventually arrives at our front desks, our airport arrival gates, and our occupancy reports.

This year’s keynote, The Next World Order, felt especially timely. 

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva re-election in Brazil and the strong Democratic showing in the US midterms are signs of a world being redrawn. 

Through a hospitality lens, that means asking:

1. Which countries will be our next source markets?
2. Where will visas get easier, and where will they tighten?
3. Which new air routes will connect Indonesia to the world?

The operators who understand the “why” behind these shifts will move faster than those who only react to the “what.”

What gave me the most hope, though, was the room itself. 

Year after year, FPCI keeps gaining momentum across universities in Indonesia, and the number of students attending, many from international relations faculties, keeps growing. 

These are the people who will one day sit at the negotiating table, and I hope some of them will help build bridges for our tourism and hospitality industry too.

Thank you to Pak Dino Patti Djalal and the entireForeign Policy Community of Indonesia team for opening our eyes to a world of seas of opportunity, not a threat.

U.S.–China Chip Restrictions: How AI Computing Is Reshaping the Global Semiconductor Landscape
The competition over artificial intelligence is no longer just about who develops the most powerful models. It is increasingly about who controls the chips, computing infrastructure, and global supply chains that make advanced AI possible
Recent developments in U.S. export policy highlight how closely semiconductor technology is connected to national security and international business
In November 2026, the U.S. government introduced new restrictions targeting access to advanced AI chips through overseas data centers. The measures also introduce additional licensing requirements for certain advanced semiconductor transfers involving Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazi
This reflects a growing concern in Washington: restricting the physical sale of advanced chips may not be sufficient if companies can access similar computing power remotely through infrastructure located in other countries
Three important implications
Advanced semiconductors are now essential infrastructure for training and operating sophisticated AI systems. Access to computing capacity can influence a company's ability to innovate, compete, and scale. As a result, governments are increasingly treating advanced computing as a strategic national asset
Countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand have attracted significant investment in data centers and digital infrastructure. However, tighter export controls could increase compliance costs, delay projects, and create uncertainty for operators serving international customers
For regional businesses, this makes regulatory transparency, customer verification, and supply-chain compliance more important than ever
Semiconductor manufacturers, cloud providers, data-center operators, and AI developers will all need to pay closer attention to where their technology is deployed and who ultimately accesses their computing resources
This is no longer simply a hardware procurement issue. It is becoming a broader question of international risk management and business strategy
My perspective
I believe the semiconductor industry is entering a period in which technological leadership and geopolitical considerations will become increasingly interconnected.
Export controls may address legitimate national security concerns, but they can also create uncertainty for businesses, affect investment decisions, and reshape global technology partnerships
At the same time, these developments may encourage countries to strengthen their domestic semiconductor capabilities and diversify their technology supply chains.
The long-term challenge is finding a balance between national security, fair competition, international cooperation, and continued innovation

The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule on 16 November, effective 19 November 2026, targeting overseas data-centre arrangements that could allow restricted foreign companies to access advanced US computing technology remotely.

The rule addresses a particular problem in semiconductor export controls: a company may be unable to import a restricted GPU directly, but could potentially rent computing capacity from a data centre in another country where those chips are installed.

The new framework introduces licensing and due-diligence requirements for certain overseas data-centre arrangements that supply significant amounts of advanced computing capacity to companies headquartered in countries of concern or Macau.

It also adds licensing requirements for specified advanced semiconductor exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil because of diversion concerns. Certain US-headquartered companies and their subsidiaries can qualify for an exception subject to reporting requirements. 

The commercial implications became clearer after Alibaba's September-quarter results. Its CEO said the new restrictions could affect products and services planned for the following year. Tencent also warned that reduced access to advanced computing resources could affect future model-training schedules. 

>> Why it matters
This extends the AI semiconductor competition beyond physical chip shipments.
Advanced AI computing is increasingly delivered as a cloud service. A customer does not necessarily need to own a GPU server; it can rent access to a cluster located thousands of kilometres away.

By addressing remote computing arrangements, Washington is attempting to control not only where advanced chips are shipped, but also who can use the computing capacity they provide.

The consequences extend to:
• Cloud providers operating data centres in third countries.
• Companies renting large GPU clusters.
Semiconductor manufacturers and distributors.
• AI developers dependent on advanced training hardware.

>> Technology explained
Consider a simplified example.
A Chinese AI company needs a large GPU cluster to train a foundation model. Direct shipment of certain advanced chips to that company may be restricted.

Instead, it rents GPU capacity from a data centre located in a third country. The servers remain physically outside China, but the customer accesses them over a network and runs training workloads remotely.

This arrangement is known as remote computing access.
The new BIS framework seeks to prevent specified restricted end users from obtaining significant advanced-computing capacity through such arrangements without the required authorisation.

The practical burden falls on data-centre operators, chip suppliers and other parties involved in the transaction. They need stronger checks on customer identity, ownership and ultimate end use.

Canva stopped posting jobs months before it restructured 22% of its staff
  
Canva stopped posting jobs before it restructured 22% of staff. Active postings fell 88% from the Feb 23, 2026 peak to Nov 2, 2026.
  
On Nov 3, Canva CEO Melanie Perkins told staff that 1,271 people, about 22% of the company, would lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs. The company has not disclosed the split between those three groups. Product, Growth and Platform are merging into one product organization, management layers are being removed, and Sydney becomes the primary home for more product teams. Perkins called it the hardest moment in the company's 13 year history, and said growth slowed in 2026 for the first time in a decade. In August Canva cut its 2026 revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20%, according to Business Insider.
  
That is the announcement. The workforce data says the hiring side of Canva turned months earlier, and that the company was still adding people, and managers, right up to the month before.
  
Job postings rolled over in the spring

Revelio Labs tracks Canva's active job postings weekly. They peaked at 3,937 in the week of Nov 3, 2025, after a surge that began the week of Sep 22, 2025. They recovered to a 2026 high of 2,496 in the week of Feb 23. By the week of Jun 22 they were at 1,504. By the week of Nov 2, 2026, the last week before the announcement, they were at 311.
  
That is a drop of 88% from the 2026 high and 79% from the Jun 22 level. Against the same week a year earlier, it is down 92%.
  
Two cautions. The weekly series is noisy, which is why the chart also shows a 4 week average. And the most recent weeks of posting data can be revised as postings are reclassified, so I would read the final reading as directional, not exact. The decline itself, from Feb through Oct, is not a single week artifact.
  
Headcount was still rising in October
  
Our modeled view of Canva's workforce went from 15,588 in Sep 2025 to 16,902 in Oct 2026, up 8.4%. Our modeled count runs well above the roughly 5,800 people implied by Canva's own 1,271 and 22% figures, so the percentages are the signal here, not the level.
  
The flow rates tell a more mixed story. All rates are trailing 12 months:
  
Hiring rate: 37.5% in Dec 2023, down to a trough of 26.1% in Aug 2025, back up to 31.6% in Oct 2026
Attrition rate: 22.1% in Sep 2024, up to 24.5% in Oct 2026
Net growth rate (hires minus exits): 15.9% in Dec 2023, 2.8% in Aug 2025, 7.2% in Oct 2026
  
The hiring rate rising while postings collapsed is not a contradiction. A trailing 12 month rate lags a weekly postings series by months. Postings are the earlier signal. The rate will show the slowdown later.
  
The management layer grew faster than the company
  
Canva said it is removing management layers. The data shows that layer grew faster than the rest of the company over the last 13 months.
  
Change in modeled headcount by seniority, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
Associate: up 22.7%
Director: up 17.7% 
Executive: up 14.8%
Manager: up 13.4% 
Entry level: up 3.0% 
Junior: down 2.9% 
  
Combine Manager, Director, Executive and Senior Executive into one layer. It went up 14.9%, against 8.1% growth for all staff with a classified seniority. That layer accounted for 37.6% of net headcount growth while representing 20.5% of the starting base. Its share of the workforce moved from 20.5% to 21.8%.
  
Our proxy for span of control, non-managers per person at manager level and above, moved from 3.87 to 3.58, a decline of 7.4%. Revelio does not observe reporting lines, so this is a proxy for organizational depth, not a count of layers.
  
Engineers and sales were the growth, design was flat
  
Change in modeled headcount by role, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
Software engineering: up 34.8% 
Research engineer: up 34.7% 
Account executive: up 20.9%
Digital marketer: up 15.4% 
Designer: up 3.9%
Web developer: down 3.9%
UX designer: down 5.0%
  
Designers are still the largest role family at about 35% of the company, but that share slipped from 36.9% to 35.4% while software engineering rose from 8.2% to 10.2%. For a company best known as a design tool, the build out of the last year was engineering and research, which fits the stated goal of building AI products.
  
Where the people are
  
Change in modeled headcount by country, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
United Kingdom: up 27.3% 
United States: up 13.9% 
Australia: up 9.6% 
Indonesia: up 7.9% 
India: down 2.1% 
Philippines: down 9.7%
  
The Philippines peaked in Jan 2026 and has fallen 10.0% since. Australia is 28.9% of the modeled workforce, close to where it started the period. Canva said product teams will concentrate in Sydney, so the geography of the 1,271 relocations and role changes is worth watching in the next few months of data.
  
What employees were already saying
  
Employee sentiment is a percentile rank against the broader dataset, built from the trailing 12 months of reviews. From Jan 2024 to Oct 2026:
  
Overall: 51 to 45
Leadership: 52 to 36
Business outlook: 50 to 39
Job security: 48 to 38
  
Leadership took the largest fall, 16 points. Review volume in the window also declined over this period, from 319 to 184, so the latest readings rest on a thinner base.
  
The talent trade
  
Over the 12 months through Oct 2026, Revelio tracked about 2,400 moves into Canva from other companies and about 1,400 out, roughly 1.7 in for every 1 out. The largest sources were Atlassian (70 in, 8 out) and Amazon (60 in, 10 out), then Microsoft and Alphabet. The largest destinations were Meta (18), Fiverr (17) and Alphabet (14). These are tracked company to company moves, and the counts for individual companies are small.
  
What I would watch next
  
Postings. Whether they stay near 300 or rebuild around the new product org. A restructuring with a hiring reset looks different from one followed by a rebuild in engineering and AI roles.
The management layer. Canva has said layers are coming out. The data to watch is whether the 3.58 non-managers per manager proxy rises back toward 3.87.
Attrition. At 24.5% before the announcement, with a 6 month severance package and the vesting cliff waived for recent hires, the survivors' exit rate in the next 2 to 3 months is the measure of how the reorganization landed.
Geography. Whether Sydney grows and the Philippines and India continue to shrink.
The split. Canva has not said how many of the 1,271 are exits versus role changes or relocations. The headcount series from Nov 2026 onward is where that will show.

What this is and is not. This is not a story about a company that was shrinking. Through Oct 2026 Canva's modeled workforce was still growing, and it was adding engineers, researchers and managers. It is a story about the sequence: the demand signal turned in the spring, the announcement came in November, and the headcount data that would confirm the cut has not yet arrived.

Yesterday, I present a talk in Indonesia Software Developer Conference (IDSW 2026) in Jakarta. It's my first national software developer conference that watched by more than 400 hundreds audience (on-site and online). To achieve this, I must submit a Call For Paper (CFP). I was nothing to lose to submit the talk. I submitted in the end of the deadline. :D
But, it turns out I'm selected. I'm very grateful of it.

I shared my experience to audience about it's (really) hard to build browser engine from scratch even with AI. The code is quite cheap this day but the understanding what's going on inside the code still matters. In the talk I give the audience the information about how many browsers we have today and what are programming languages uses to build the browser engine. Mostly C/C++ and Rust.

I pick the another choice which is Swift programming language. The most reason I choose Swift programming language because Swift has SwiftUI and AppKit that be used as desktop app. Because, in the end, the end-users is a consumer of desktop app so they can see it visually. Also, Swift's performance is amazing and can be fast as C/C++ and Rust.

The talk focused on how to achieve smooth scrolling near to 60 fps and resize the browser near to 60 fps. FPS (Frame Per Second) play the important part here because the end-user want to see smooth experience when they interact with the content. It means I need to make 1 frame finish in 16.7 ms. If more than that then it will be a terrible experience.

After the talk, I reflected again that there are some parts that I cannot deliver in detail to the audience like telling them why the slow scroll happen, why slow resize happen, and what's the invalidation list (related with cache invalidation). I'm bit regret. But, it covered by the demoing the browser and headless browser into the audience.

Well, for the part that I cannot deliver in detail, I will atone my sin into the separated video and blog post.

The funny thing is my title is Senior Backend Developer but what I present to audiences is not aligned with my profession. :D Well, title just title. :D

Lastly, I would like to say thank you very much for the organizers to organize this great conference. Nothing is perfect! But, they're deliver well. Keep improving as always. Thank you.  😊

If you're an Android developer, read this 👇

From January, Android starts making it harder to install apps from developers Google can't identify.

Google has been running this since September 30 in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. 

In January it goes global with seven app stores, including Play, Galaxy Store, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo, and over the following months it will cover every country and every way of installing an app on a certified Android phone.

The reason is malware. Google's own analysis found over 90 times more malware in sideloaded apps than in apps from Play.

If your app is only on Play and your account is already verified, you mostly don't need to do anything, because Google registers those apps for you.

The teams that need to pay attention are the ones shipping outside Play. That means APKs people download from your website, apps on OEM stores, internal apps for field staff, and test builds you send to clients.

Once this is live, installing an unregistered app gets harder. The user has to go through an advanced flow and accept a risk warning, and a lot of users will back out at that screen. Each of those is an install you lose.

What I'd do this month:
- Check the registration status of every package in Play Console, including apps you distribute outside Play
- If you're not on Play, create an Android Developer Console account. Registering takes under ten minutes per app
- If you manage many apps, automate registration in your CI pipeline with the Developer ID Status and Developer Console APIs
- For test builds, use a limited distribution account. It covers up to 50 devices, with no fee and no ID check

ADB installs stay the same, so your developers' daily work doesn't change.

Right now this is a ten-minute job. A few months from now, skipping it will cost you installs every time a user sees that warning.

I’m happy to share that I attended the Automation Webinar: UiPath x IOH on November 19, 2026, organized by ONE Indonesia in partnership with UiPath and Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison. 

There are two sessions in this webinar :

Automation in the AI Era, with Irwan Almarus Kausar, Ph.D. (Lecturer Universitas Muhammadiyah Sidoarjo)
Chatbots, agents, and automation are not the same thing. Automation follows a defined flow: Trigger → Extract Data → Process → Decision → Action → Report. It also enables collaboration across tools through standards like Model Context Protocol (MCP). My biggest takeaway: combine rules (cheap, fast, consistent) with AI models (flexible), while humans stay in control as the “goalkeeper” who sets goals, rules, and approvals.

Practical RPA with UiPath, with Dipo Atri (RPA Developer, ONE Indonesia)
In a live UiPath Studio demo, a robot read Gmail messages, extracted the data, filled in Google Sheets and Google Forms, and automatically sent a report by email. The best processes to automate are repetitive, manual, and rule-based. Data validation and recovery design need to be planned from the start.

Thank you to ONE Indonesia, UiPath, Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, and the speakers for sharing their knowledge! 🙏

The era of the borderless cloud just ended.

For four years, Washington tried to win the AI race by controlling where physical chips were shipped.

There was just one billion-dollar loophole: you do not need to smuggle a server rack across a border when you can rent its compute power over a subsea fiber-optic cable.

In the span of four days last week, the US and its allies closed that door permanently:

November 15: The US, India, Japan, South Korea, the UK, Australia, Israel, Singapore, the UAE, and Qatar signed the San Francisco Declaration under the Pax Silica alliance.

November 19: The US Commerce Department issued a rule treating remote generative AI training on US-origin chips in Southeast Asia and Brazil as a controlled export.

One is the velvet rope. The other is the bouncer.

Here is why every tech leader, investor, and policy strategist needs to update their mental map right now:

→ Jurisdictional trust is now a line item in cloud unit economics. For a decade, data center architects optimized for power, cooling, and latency. Starting this quarter, geopolitical alignment carries equal weight.

→ The "neutral cloud hub" model is over. Operators in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil have 90 days to comply with strict licensing and workload verification or cut off restricted clients.

→ India just got a major infrastructure tailwind. As a founding Pax Silica signatory with massive developer scale and zero appetite for hosting restricted workloads, Mumbai, Chennai, and Hyderabad suddenly look far more attractive to global hyperscalers than probationary hubs in Southeast Asia.

The global internet is no longer just splitting over content moderation. It is splitting at the physical silicon and cloud infrastructure layer into three competing compute blocs.

𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐋𝐞𝐧𝐬: 𝐂𝐚𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐛𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐩 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐚 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐚𝐫?

A floating solar project needs financing before it generates its first megawatt-hour.

So what changes when part of its revenue depends on the emissions it cuts after it comes online?

At COP31, Indonesia’s state-owned utility PLN and the Global Green Growth Institute, acting on Norway’s behalf, signed Indonesia’s first purchase agreement for emissions reductions under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. The initial focus is floating solar paired with battery storage.*

Under the agreement, Norway can purchase up to 12 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in emissions reductions over ten years. Payment depends on the reductions being achieved, verified and delivered. They must also go beyond what would have happened without the programme.**

The agreement supports Indonesia’s Generation-Based Incentive programme. Its purpose is to help eligible projects proceed when the standard price paid for their electricity falls short. 

The programme tracks how much electricity a project generates and supplies to the grid, and an independent audit checks those records before operators receive performance-based payments.***

That creates a practical question for developers. How much of that future carbon revenue can a project count on when it needs to raise money upfront?

If the grid connection is delayed, the project may start earning that revenue later than planned. If it delivers less electricity than expected, it may earn less. Both scenarios belong in the project’s financial model from the start.

The programme also needs to show which projects the incentive helps bring forward. A project that would already proceed at the existing power price has a different case from one that only becomes viable with the extra revenue.

The measure of success will be how many projects the agreement helps get built and how much they actually reduce emissions once they start supplying power to the grid.

* Indonesia Ministry of Environment and Environmental Control Agency, COP31 CarbonNex closing release, 21 November 2026.  
** Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment, New programme to cut emissions from Indonesia’s power sector, 16 November 2026.  
*** Global Green Growth Institute, Indonesia Accelerates Energy Transition with Landmark Carbon Market Agreement at COP31, 11 November 2026.

At the 2026 FIP Junior Asia Padel Cup, young athletes had the chance to represent their countries, test themselves against international opponents, and spend a week getting to know players from other nations. For a club or venue developer, that raises a practical question early in a project: How will junior players actually use the facility once it opens? A court can host an international event for a week. A junior programme needs reliable court time, coaching, and regular opportunities to play throughout the year.

For us at Fortune Sport, that’s a reason to discuss junior programmes with venue partners during project planning. Knowing who will train there, how often they’ll play, and how the club will run its coaching sessions gives the project team a clearer brief for the facility.

📌 Export controls and foundries
Under the Nov. 19 rule, covered chip transfers generally require a license if the exporter knows a data center will provide over 12 million TPP in computing capacity to a company headquartered in Macau or a Group D:5 country, including China. It also applies if the company’s ultimate parent is headquartered there. Capacity is counted across linked sites. Existing providers have 90 days to obtain a license to continue covered services.
Separate controls apply to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, with an exemption for qualifying U.S.-headquartered firms and their subsidiaries.
Reuters reported that TSMC told some Chinese chip designers it would halt affected orders at 16 nm and below without a U.S. license. The Financial Times reported that Samsung Electronics also paused some shipments to Chinese customers.
📌 Earnings and manufacturing
NVIDIA’s fiscal Q3 revenue reached $115.8 billion. Data Center revenue rose 110% year over year to $107.6 billion. Its Q4 revenue forecast of $130 billion (±3%) assumes no Data Center compute sales to China. Kinsus plans to expand its NVIDIA-dedicated ABF substrate capacity to over 3.5 times current levels. NVIDIA’s July and October deals with Amkor total nearly $3 billion, including prepayments.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company had signed its first external 18A customer. Its CTO identified the process as 18A-P. Intel did not name the customer or give a production date.
📌 Memory and devices
TrendForce expects NAND contract prices to hold steady or fall by up to 5% in Q1 2027 from the prior quarter, with declines across all categories from Q2. It forecasts 2027 NAND capital spending of $29.9 billion, up 26.7%. South Korea’s Maeil Business Newspaper reported that Apple and Samsung Electronics were close to a long-term DRAM supply deal.
SK hynix and its government partners are funding Trinity Fab, a ₩874.6 billion test line for suppliers in Yongin. In Southeast Asia, Q3 smartphone shipments fell 36% year over year to 16.5 million units, while the average selling price rose 53%, according to Omdia.
📌 California AI policy
A Nov. 18 state report proposes giving California the power to order an AI model shut down if danger is imminent and the developer refuses to act. It recommends cutting the reporting deadline for most critical safety incidents from 15 days to 48 hours, while keeping the 24-hour deadline for imminent catastrophic risks.
Separately, Attorney General Rob Bonta served NVIDIA with an investigative subpoena on Nov. 19.

Sarawak’s Energy Expansion to Drive IPP and Infrastructure Opportunities Through 2035.

Sarawak is positioning itself as a major regional energy hub, with further Independent Power Producer (IPP) awards expected through 2030 as the state accelerates its electricity generation expansion. According to Kenanga Research’s November 2026 thematic report, Sarawak Energy plans to increase generation capacity from approximately 6GW currently to 10GW by 2030 and 15GW by 2035, creating substantial opportunities for private investors, developers and engineering contractors.

POWER GENERATION AND INFRASTRUCTURE EXPANSION
The near-term capacity expansion will be supported by two combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) plants in Samalaju and Miri, with a combined capacity of up to 2GW. The 1,285MW Baleh Hydroelectric Project is expected to commence operations by 2030. Singapore is identified as a potential major electricity buyer, followed by West Kalimantan, Indonesia.

SOLAR IPP OPPORTUNITIES
Sarawak has already awarded or placed approximately 950MW of solar capacity under development, leaving another 550MW for private-sector participation to achieve its 1.5GW target by 2030. The remaining awards could be accelerated over the next one to two years.

If solar capacity expands to 2.2–3.7GW by 2035, the estimated Engineering, Procurement, Construction and Commissioning (EPCC) market could reach RM7.3–12.2 billion.

CASCADING HYDROPOWER DEVELOPMENT
Sarawak Energy has invited proposals for five priority river basins under its Cascading Power Sources (CPS) hydropower model. Final Investment Decisions are realistically expected from 2027, with EPCC activities potentially commencing in the second half of 2027 or 2028. The five projects could involve construction expenditure of up to RM16.7 billion, with full operations targeted for 2034–2035.

PRIVATE-SECTOR PARTICIPATION AND CONTRACTING OPPORTUNITIES
Kenanga identifies two major investment avenues:

1. Asset ownership: Opportunities for companies such as Ibraco, Pansar and Solarvest to participate in solar IPPs, CPS hydropower projects and water-treatment infrastructure, potentially through joint ventures and strategic partnerships.

2. EPCC contracting: Companies such as Hartanah Kenyalang and Kee Ming Group could benefit from contracts covering solar installations, substations, electrical infrastructure and civil engineering works.

Last week, Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs raised $47M led byAccel in India to collect real-world data for robotics. Similar players are appearing worldwide. Here's how I see it.

How we read markets
At Genesia Ventures, we use a simple market lens called Ignition iO, adapted from Ohm's law (I = V/R). V is demand pressure: how badly buyers need something. R stands for resistance: what holds that demand back from becoming a scalable business. A market discontinuously ignites only when R falls against strong V. We've published a compass for new-business hypotheses built on it, Ignition Compass, and use it across our four markets: Japan, Indonesia, Vietnam and India.

https://lnkd.in/gvfrB4um

A quick read of this market:
Here, V is US robot-model developers needing real human task data. Primary R, the one resistance holding the whole market back, was technology. It fell in 2025–26, when robot models became limited by data rather than architecture. India can also build on decades of US–India ties in IT services and startups.
 
But R fell for every vendor. So the question isn't whether demand comes. It's who executes better, and who builds something that compounds.

My hypothesis
The pure data-generation step will commoditise. Hours of footage, country coverage and capture devices are a capital game, and synthetic data will push prices down further. Value moves to the steps around it:
 
Before: knowing which data actually improves a model, and defining the task itself. Shop-floor procedures captured once can be reused across an industry, and India's industrial clusters are an edge here.
After: how robots perform and fail at real sites, which labs can't see from their own buildings.
 
So synthetic data isn't the threat it seems. Simulation is weakest where work is messy and contact-heavy: garments, food processing, wiring, construction.
 
If I were starting today, I'd go narrow and deep: one contact-heavy industry, entered by running remote operations from India, around the clock, for robots already deployed at customer sites. India built this model in IT and BPO. Every intervention becomes the failure data that labs want most, and revenue recurs.

Where a Japan-born VC can help
This thesis isn't new for us. We led FastLabel株式会社's seed round in 2021 and have backed it ever since, as it grew into one of Japan's leading AI data companies.
 
Japanese manufacturing and construction are losing skilled workers, and much of their know-how lives only in veterans' hands or brains. They need procedure capture and robot deployment, in exactly the environments simulation handles worst. We can open those doors: Japanese manufacturers and construction firms as customers and deployment sites, plus a "GENBA" (shop-floor) culture of documenting and improving work that maps directly onto this business. We see ourselves alongside top India-US investors, not instead of them.
 
If you're building or investing here, I'd love to compare notes!

Landmark proposal by Google andOhio Power Company offers a compelling blueprint for how#utilities &#hyperscalers can solve this gridlock without burdening everyday taxpayers and 4 strategic lessons for#Indonesia’s energy & digital transition

Rather than waiting years for traditional public capital cycles, Google is voluntarily funding the $10.8 million incremental cost to upgrade 15.5 miles of aging Columbus power lines with advanced, higher-capacity conductors—alongside $1 million for lineman training and supply chain apprenticeships

✅Result: win-win regulatory model. Google accelerates its contracted power delivery by two years, the grid eventually unlocks over 700 MW of additional capacity, and everyday taxpayers actually see slightly lower transmission costs due to reduced line losses

✅As Indonesia accelerates its rise as Southeast Asia’s premier digital infrastructure hub from #GreaterJakarta to#Batam—policymakers PT PLN (Persero) & industry leaders should study this model closely.

Indonesia faces a classic infrastructure trilemma: 
✅Surging industrial & data center demand
✅Complex land-acquisition timelines ✅Socioeconomic imperative to keep electricity affordable for citizens

4 strategic lessons stand out for Indonesia’s energy and digital transition:

1. Institutionalize Corporate Co-Funding Frameworks

Indonesia’sMinistry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM) &PLN Indonesia Power can pioneer "transmission participation agreements." Allowing hyperscalers & industrial estates to co-fund incremental grid upgrades in exchange for expedited interconnection relieves capital pressure on the state budget while accelerating foreign direct investment

2. Prioritize Reconductoring Over Greenfield Expansion

Building new high-voltage corridors often stalls due to right-of-way & land acquisition hurdles. Replacing legacy wires on existing towers with advanced conductors (reconductoring) unlocks massive latent capacity in a fraction of the time—turning existing assets into high-efficiency arteries

3. Turn Hyperscale Demand into a Ratepayer Dividend

Grid upgrades for big tech shouldn't socialize costs onto households. By structuring agreements where corporate off-takers absorb the marginal cost of advanced hardware, Indonesia can improve grid reliability & lower line losses—passing systemic efficiencies directly to everyday consumers

4. Pair Physical Capex with Human Capital & Local Supply Chains

Advanced grid hardware is only as scalable as the workforce installing it. Indonesia should tie major data center and energy concessions to co-funded vocational curricula for PLN engineers linemen

By shifting from purely state-funded infrastructure to collaborative, performance-based grid modernization, Indonesia can power its digital economy while strengthening its public utility foundation

We split the module into four sessions, one system:
🔹 Part 1, End-to-end architecture: terrestrial backhaul, cable landing station, dry plant and wet plant in one big picture
🔹 Part 2, Wet plant: cable armour, fibre pairs, repeaters and branching units
🔹 Part 3, Dry plant: SLTE, PFE, DWDM, coherent transmission, NMS and COTDR
🔹 Part 4, System integration: capacity, redundancy, protection, open cable and what's next

What made these two days special was the participants' enthusiasm. Hands went up for every question, the questions kept coming in every session. Instead of a one-way lecture, it became a real conversation and discussion between engineers in the field and the next-gen engineers.

For an archipelago of 17,000+ islands, submarine cables are not a niche topic. They are the backbone of our digital economy. Seeing this many next-gen engineers curious about it gives us a lot of hope for the industry.

In 2018, I wrote a blog post about getting a medical check-up for my Taiwan resident visa. Eight years later, I hold an APRC, and many of the rules have changed in favour of foreign talent.
 
Here's what I wish someone had told me back then, updated for 2026:
 
The 15-day clock is real. If you enter Taiwan on a resident visa, you must apply for your ARC within 15 days. Put it in your calendar the day you land.
You may not need a resident visa first. Foreign professionals entering visa-free or on a visitor visa can, in many cases, apply for an ARC directly.
Health certificates depend on your passport. Whether you or your family need one depends on your nationality and residence category, and it must usually be issued within the last 3 months. Coming from Indonesia, I learned to start this step early.
Permanent residency is closer than you think. Foreign professionals can apply for an APRC after 5 years of continuous legal residence, averaging 183 days a year, not 183 days in every single year. A degree from a Taiwanese university can shorten that by 1 to 3 years.
APRC gives you real flexibility. Foreign professionals holding an APRC can work in Taiwan without a separate work permit, which also makes hiring simpler for employers.
 
Taiwan has become one of the more welcoming places in Asia for international professionals. The paperwork still takes patience, but knowing the rules early saves a lot of stress.
 
Requirements vary by situation, so always confirm with the National Immigration Agency or the Ministry of Labor.

A lot of you ask me how to figure out what to post on LinkedIn. I spent 2 hours in a LinkedIn masterclass by THE Lara Acosta on a Sunday night, so you don’t have to 😂 

If you don’t know Lara, she made Forbes 30 Under 30 list, built 7-figure businesses onLinkedIn and helped 5,000+ people build their personal brands. I mean, what a role model, right??

Now, let me spill the tea for you 👀🍵

The idea: your unfair advantage sits where these three overlap.
1/ Scars. What you overcame.
2/ Skills. What's easy for you, hard for everyone else.
3/ Proof. What you can actually show for it.

I did the exercise live, on myself. Here's what came out.

🙃 Scars: What have you been through that changed how you do things?
- I moved from Jakarta, Indonesia to Bonn, Germany without speaking any German and had to rebuild my network from the ground up. 
- Almost got unemployed after 2.5 years in the same corporation despite having worked across 4 teams, 2 job functions across 2 countries where I constantly have to prove myself each time.
-Recently, I found myself as the non-technical PM in a room full of AI engineers and architects. 

🤝 Skills: What comes naturally to you that other people find hard?
For me, it’s connecting with strangers (which is really friends waiting to happen), building with AI, translating technical concepts into business impact, embracing change (never thought about how handy this actually is), and connecting dots between things that don’t obviously go together. 
And writing on LinkedIn, not Lara-level yet, but I'll get there ☺️

🏅 Proof: What can you actually show for it?
I've turned coffee chats into jobs, LinkedIn cold outreaches into speaking opportunities, and a coworking space chat into real friendship (this one I'm most proud of).
I built a web app from scratch that got 183 visits in 2 weeks. 
I wrote a post that got over 17,000 impressions.

Doing this exercise out loud made me realize my actual story was never about AI or the tools I use. It's about sharing the things only I've experienced and how it shaped my thinking and my career path.

This is 1 of 3 frameworks I took from the masterclass that felt useful to me as a Gen Z woman in tech working in corporate. Thank YOU for the immense knowledge-sharing session,Lara! YOU ROCK!! 👏

Btw, if you’re early in your career and figuring out what to share here too, follow along for the other 2 ☺️ And tell me what your biggest challenge with posting is!

If AI writes 80% of the code, who should be responsible for the remaining 100% of the outcome?

AI can generate components, write functions, fix errors, and even suggest architectural decisions in seconds.

What happens when:

This is where a developer's role still matters.

AI can speed up implementation, but understanding requirements, reviewing code, making technical decisions, testing edge cases, and taking responsibility for production outcomes still require engineering judgment.

The rupiah touched 18,289 to the US dollar last week, a record low. A year ago it was around 16,675.

Take a Jakarta customer who renewed at the same rupiah price. No discount, no churn, no downgrade. In dollars that contract is now worth 16,675 / 18,289 = 0.91 of what it was. About 9% of USD ARR gone without anyone in sales doing anything wrong.

The cost side does not move with it. Cloud, AI tools and most developer tooling are billed in dollars. If dollar costs were 25% of revenue (say), gross margin slips from 75% to 72.6% on the same customers using the product the same way.

FX cuts both ways. Karooooo grew Cartrack ARR 19% in rand in its latest quarter and 30% in dollars. Same business, 11 points of difference from the currency alone.

In my view the USD growth rate is the least useful number to judge an emerging-market software business on. I would put constant-currency ARR next to the share of costs that sit in dollars. A business that earns in pesos and rupiah and also pays its engineers, support and payroll specialists in the region carries a natural hedge that a dollar headline hides.

Constant-currency ARR growth and the dollar share of COGS. Those are the two numbers I would ask for first.
